clue.text: Shop left for conversion to strip club?

indicators.note: a building up for conversion is about to be remodelled, so the letters get rebuilt into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A high-street shop is left empty and turned into a strip club.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a planning story, and the conversion is of letters, not premises. A fleshpot is a place of sensual indulgence; the question mark admits a strip club is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleshpot is any venue offering sleazy entertainment, so a stripping establishment is one example of the kind.

clue.text: See 6
See 6
Matched church for love in ecclesiastical council

indicators.note: 'church for love' reads as church in exchange for love, one thing swapped in where the other was

blocks.note: a synod is a governing assembly of a church
CE = Church of England
love = nil = O, from tennis scoring

explanation.surface: A church council pairs up couples, trading religion for romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church for love' means put the church in place of the love: the O in SYNOD goes and CE takes its seat.
explanation.definitionFit: To be synced is to be synchronised or brought into step, which is to be paired or aligned with another thing.

clue.text: Wrecked ship man has study not completed

indicators.note: a study not completed stops short, so the word meaning study loses its final letter

blocks.note: 'man has' = he's
PERUSE, to study, without its final letter

explanation.surface: A shipwrecked sailor who never finished his studies.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wreck of the Hesperus is a Longfellow poem, and in Britain 'looking like the wreck of the Hesperus' is a stock phrase for being dishevelled.
explanation.definitionFit: The schooner in Longfellow's famous ballad runs aground in a storm and breaks up on a reef, a literary shipwreck.

clue.text: From 8 28, 18A, seen drunk with 22A, flattery achieves little

indicators.note: someone seen drunk is staggering all over the place, so the combined letters of the three answers reel into a new order

blocks.note: the answer to 8 down and 28 across, the Cumbrian town
the answer to 18 across
the answer to 22 across

explanation.surface: A man called Des from a Cumbrian town is spotted drunk with his tankard, sweet-talking to no avail.
explanation.walkthrough: The three cross-referenced answers supply exactly 25 letters between them, and 'seen drunk' scrambles them. The proverb is an old British saying: fine words butter no parsnips means talk alone gets nothing done.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says pleasant talk cannot improve a plain meal, so compliments and sweet talk accomplish nothing practical.

clue.text: Enchanting area within reach across river

indicators.note: a word stretched across the river spans it, so the river letter ends up held inside

blocks.note: A = area
something within reach can be done
R = river

explanation.surface: A charming spot lies within easy reach across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Within reach' reads as location but is a single idea, doable; that phrase then stretches 'across' the river letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something so charming and delightful that people are captivated by it.

clue.text: Pub dispute getting heated audibly in Cumbrian town

indicators.note: 'audibly' asks us to hear the phrase for getting heated said out loud and spell the place name that sounds the same

blocks.note: a bar is a pub
a row is a quarrel
something in a furnace is getting heated

explanation.surface: An argument in a pub turns heated in a small northern English town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting heated' looks like it describes the dispute, but it is its own piece. Barrow-in-Furness is a shipbuilding town on the Cumbrian coast of north-west England, on the Furness peninsula.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the name of a port and shipbuilding town in the county of Cumbria, England.

clue.text: Characters warped in occult eye cell that protects

indicators.note: the characters are the letters of the phrase that follows, and warping bends them out of their original order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters, the 'characters' of the phrase

explanation.surface: Strange characters bent out of shape in an occult eye symbol serve as a protective charm.
explanation.walkthrough: The occult imagery points to talismans, but the protection is biological. 'Characters' just says it is the letters of 'occult eye' that get warped.
explanation.definitionFit: A leucocyte is a white blood cell, part of the immune system that defends the body against infection.

clue.text: Home help sent to West Country I may represent

indicators.note: in an across clue west is leftwards, so help sent west is written from right to left

blocks.note: at home = in
aid = help

explanation.surface: A domestic helper is dispatched to the West Country, where they might act as a local representative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West Country' reads as the English region, but 'West' belongs to the reversal and 'Country' to the definition. In an across clue, going west means right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet the letter I is spoken as the name of this South Asian nation.

clue.text: Sanskrit rule oddly disregarded is just great

indicators.note: letters in odd positions are ignored, leaving only the second, fourth, sixth and so on of the phrase

blocks.note: the even letters of the phrase, once the odd ones are ignored

explanation.surface: Someone declares that ignoring an ancient rule now and then is simply wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is just great' reads as a verdict on the rule but is the fodder: drop the first, third, fifth letters and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: A sutra is an aphorism or set of precepts in Hindu or Buddhist scripture, written in the classical Indian language.

clue.text: Copper and lead are carried in on back for attendant

indicators.note: 'on back' means the word for on is sent backwards, read right to left
the word 'are' is carried inside the turned word, so that word holds it

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
re = on, concerning
taken as it stands

explanation.surface: Metal is lugged in on someone's back, as a porter might carry it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' and 'lead' are the chemical symbols, a standard crossword source of letters. 'On' means regarding, the sense of re in a business letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cupbearer was a royal servant whose job was to pour and serve wine, so an official attendant at court.

clue.text: Put right in pub when alongside news boss

indicators.note: 'when alongside news boss' places the word for when directly next to the editor, one after the other

blocks.note: PH = public house, as on maps
R = right
as = when
ed = editor, the boss of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor sets things right while drinking in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put right' looks like one phrase meaning fixed, but 'Put' alone is the definition, as in 'put it tactfully'.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something a certain way is to express it in words, which is exactly what phrasing does.

clue.text: Spectral deity visiting E3?

definitions.note: adjective for a noun answer used attributively, as in rainbow colours

blocks.note: Ra is the Egyptian sun god
visiting = in
E3 is the London postcode of Bow

explanation.surface: A ghostly god drops in on an East London postcode.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spectral' suggests ghosts but means of the spectrum. Bow is a district of East London whose postcode is E3; the question mark flags a clue by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A rainbow spreads sunlight into its full band of colours, so it is the spectrum made visible in the sky.

clue.text: Vincent's content with journal being scandalous?

indicators.note: a name's content is what sits inside it, so we keep the inner letters and drop the first and last

blocks.note: the inside of Vincent without its outer letters
a diary is a journal

explanation.surface: The contents of Vincent's private journal turn out to be shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as what Vincent wrote, and is the letters inside his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Something incendiary is inflammatory, likely to provoke outrage, as a shocking revelation does.

clue.text: Is heel turned to show bones in foot?

indicators.note: the phrase 'Is heel' is turned around end to end, so its letters are read backwards

blocks.note: taken as it stands
a heel is a scoundrel, a rat

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether turning the heel exposes the bones of the foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heel' sits in a clue about feet but means a rotter. The whole phrase 'Is heel' is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarsals are the cluster of small ankle bones at the back of the human skeleton's lower limb.

clue.text: Those going on walks they go on?

blocks.note: people who hike through the countryside for pleasure
people who talk on and on without getting to the point

explanation.surface: A riddle about walkers and the things they keep doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on' is used twice in two senses: to set out on a walk, and to talk at tedious length.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambler is both a leisure hiker in the countryside and a person who talks aimlessly at length.

clue.text: Some French bloke

blocks.note: the French partitive article for 'some' before a plural
a man's name, short for Desmond

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for a Frenchman, but 'Some French' is the French word for 'some'. Crosswords treat any short male name as a 'bloke' or 'man'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the plural article meaning 'some' in French and a common diminutive of Desmond.

clue.text: Parliament to quote rises based on consumption

indicators.note: in a down clue a word that rises is read from bottom to top, so the word for quote goes backwards

blocks.note: a diet is a legislative assembly, as in some European countries
to cite is to quote

explanation.surface: A parliament votes to raise prices according to how much gets used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rises' suggests prices going up; in a down clue it turns the quoted word upwards. 'Consumption' means eating, not economics.
explanation.definitionFit: Dietetic means relating to diet and nutrition, the science of what people eat.

clue.text: Press covering last letter from George Best

indicators.note: the word for press goes over and around the selected letter, covering it
the phrase asks literally for the final character of the name that follows it

blocks.note: to cram is to press or squeeze in
the final letter of George

explanation.surface: The newspapers report on a final letter from the footballer George Best.
explanation.walkthrough: George Best was a famous Manchester United footballer, but the name splits: George gives a letter and 'Best' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream of something is its finest part, the elite, as cream rises to the top of milk.

clue.text: Rocky height appears in wet for one at wheel

indicators.note: the rocky height shows up inside the word for wet, placed within it

blocks.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
moist = wet

explanation.surface: A craggy peak looms out of rain, which matters to someone driving.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky outcrop on a hilltop, common on the moors of south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorist is a car driver, the person sitting behind the steering control.

clue.text: Land ownership seemed suspect with northern resident

indicators.note: something suspect is dodgy or not right, so the letters of seemed are rearranged
a resident lives inside a home, so the northern letter lives inside the scrambled word

blocks.note: anagram fodder
N = northern

explanation.surface: A land claim looks dodgy because of someone living up north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resident' looks like a person but tells the northern letter to live inside the scrambled word.
explanation.definitionFit: Demesne is a legal term for possession of land as one's own, and for an estate held that way.

clue.text: Repudiate Pluto, now reviewed

indicators.note: a revised word has been gone over and reworked, so the letters of now are reshuffled

blocks.note: Dis is another name for Pluto, Roman god of the underworld
taken as it stands

explanation.surface: Astronomers reconsider and reject Pluto, echoing its demotion from planet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Pluto losing planet status in 2006, but here Pluto is the Roman god of the dead, also called Dis.
explanation.definitionFit: To disown and to repudiate both mean refusing to acknowledge any connection with something or someone.

clue.text: Best advice given about caressing new tankard

indicators.note: advice given about is turned round, so the phrase for best advice is read backwards
to caress is to hold fondly in an embrace, so the letter for new is held inside

blocks.note: the best advice is a top tip
N = new

explanation.surface: Someone offers the best advice on how to fondle a new beer mug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best advice' is a stock phrase, top tip, which turned round becomes PIT POT; the new letter then nestles inside the first half.
explanation.definitionFit: A pint pot is a drinking vessel holding a pint, typically a pewter or glass beer mug with a handle.

clue.text: Smoke rings to divert

indicators.note: as a verb, to ring is to encircle, so the word for smoke surrounds the next word

blocks.note: to puff is to smoke
taken as it stands

explanation.surface: A smoker blows smoke rings to distract someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoke rings' looks like one noun, but 'rings' is a verb telling the smoke to surround the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone off is to distract them or deflect them from their purpose.

clue.text: Father Time stops glib talk

indicators.note: time stops the father as a cork stops a bottle, plugging a gap inside it

blocks.note: pater is Latin for father, old British public-school slang
T = time

explanation.surface: Old Father Time puts an end to smooth chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father Time' is a familiar figure, but it splits in two; 'stops' means plugs, as a stopper fills a bottle's neck.
explanation.definitionFit: Patter is the rapid, practised chat of a salesman or comedian, smooth and superficial speech.

clue.text: Fishmonger possibly the only supplier?

blocks.note: a trader whose business is a particular flatfish
the single firm with exclusive rights to sell a product

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is a whimsical one: someone who deals in the flatfish sole. 'Possibly' flags that a fishmonger is only one way to read it.
explanation.definitionFit: A business with exclusive distribution rights in an area is the one and only seller of that product.

clue.text: Small monkey's grabbed in domed recess

indicators.note: 'monkey's grabbed' is monkey has grabbed, so the monkey word clutches the small letter inside itself

blocks.note: S = small
an ape stands in for monkey

explanation.surface: A little monkey is caught hiding in an alcove under a dome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monkey's' is monkey has: the monkey has grabbed the small letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a semicircular vaulted recess at the end of a church, usually roofed with a half-dome.

clue.text: Menacing playwright leaves piano in Bury

indicators.note: piano leaves the playwright's name, meaning that letter departs and is removed from it

blocks.note: Harold Pinter, whose plays were called comedies of menace
p = piano, quietly in music

explanation.surface: A sinister dramatist drops his piano off in Bury, a town near Manchester.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a Lancashire town, so 'in Bury' reads as a place; the capital hides the verb. Harold Pinter's plays are known for their air of menace.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to place a dead body in a grave, which is exactly what burying means.
